source.title: On Double Descent in Reinforcement Learning with LSTD and Random Features
source.authors: David Brellmann; Eloïse Berthier; David Filliat; Goran Frehse

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. There is a stray garbled string after the Figure 5 caption; it does not make the text unusable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests capacity-dependent double descent in a new setting: regularized LSTD with random features for reinforcement-learning value estimation, measured using true MSBE. It does not directly test deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper sweeps feature count relative to distinct visited states and reports true MSBE results. Empirical MSBE is a training-data measure, so it is not cataloged as a test-risk result. The correction-factor diagnostics explain the reported behavior but are not themselves test-risk outcomes. The number of transitions n is stated in settings but is not swept as a test of more-data-hurts; changing m, the number of distinct visited states, is not the same as a sample-size sweep.
record.test_reason: Sweeps random-feature count N relative to distinct visited states m for regularized LSTD in RL policy evaluation. It reports true MSBE peaking near N=m and falling again for N>m, plus how l2 regularization removes the peak. This is a new model class and setting for model-wise double descent (V4) and its regularization dependence (V6). It is not a deep-network test (V1).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors derive deterministic limits for empirical and true MSBE in regularized random-feature LSTD as N and m grow with fixed ratio. They find correction terms that produce a true-MSBE peak at N=m, while empirical MSBE shows none. The peak vanishes with larger l2 regularization or when no states are left unvisited, and the discount factor has little effect. Extensions to deep networks, off-policy learning and other RL algorithms are left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and evaluates regularized LSTD with random features in reinforcement learning, rather than testing a deep-network supervised-learning recipe. The paper does not specify an original-method recipe for direct comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak changes with l2 regularization and the number of distinct unvisited states. The discount factor has little reported effect in the tested Gridworld setting.

fits_no_version.finding: The interpolation threshold sits at N equal to the number of distinct visited states m, not the number of transitions n. The peak is driven by unvisited states, vanishing when m=|S|, rather than by label noise. Empirical (training) MSBE shows no double descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TD/LSTD value estimation, the double-descent peak is located at parameters = distinct visited states. It arises from states absent from the training data and disappears when all states are visited.

record.problems: The experiments are random-feature LSTD on synthetic and small MRP environments, not deep networks. Experiments average over 30 instances; numerical curve values in the supplied text are figure-only. The true-MSBE result relies on stated assumptions, including an assumption controlling the empirical transition model. No epoch sweep, transition-sample-size sweep, or label-noise intervention is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for empirical MSBE: it measures error on collected transitions, not the true-MSBE risk used for the double-descent result. Correction-factor plots and the second-order correction term are mechanistic diagnostics rather than test-risk outcomes. The paper's additional MSVE results are outside the claim's stated test-error/MSBE measure.

untested.parts: There are no deep networks. Random features approximate a single-hidden-layer network in the lazy regime only.
There is no sweep over epochs or training time; LSTD is solved in closed form.
The number of transitions n is not swept as a sample-size axis for test MSBE.
There is no test of a single complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epoch and sample axes.
Label or reward noise is not manipulated, and no multiple or triple descent is reported. λ is not shown to be optimally tuned; only that larger λ removes the peak.
There is no recounting of effective parameters to turn the second descent into a U-curve.

missing.what: True MSVE (value error) versus N/m at three λ values shows the same double-descent peak at N=m that vanishes with larger λ. This is arguably the closest analogue to test risk and bears on V4 and V6.
Discount-factor sweep (γ=0, 0.5, 0.95, 0.99) in all three MRPs at λ=1e-9, 1e-6 and 1e-3. γ=0 is the supervised-learning special case.
True MSBE as a function of λ at N/m=0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 for n=1000, 3000 and 5000. At N=m, MSBE decreases as λ increases.

record.verdict_notes: The record linked the visited-state rows at fixed λ to V6; these bear only on V4. Several λ=1e-3 rows were labelled absent without curve-specific text, so they are reset to cannot_determine. Figure values are figure-only, and results average 30 random-feature seeds on one data path (seed 42). The theory relies on Assumption 3 about the empirical transition model.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random features in LSTD, not deep networks, and does not test the claim for deep-network model size.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No test of increasing the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold. Varying distinct visited states m does not establish this.
Tested for random-feature LSTD in RL using true MSBE, not across a broad range of model classes or with ordinary supervised test error.
The study uses N/m as model complexity, but does not test whether one measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample-size axes.
Tests how increasing l2 regularization affects the peak. Does not test label-noise or variance causation, multiple or triple descent, or optimally tuned regularization.
Does not re-count complexity using an alternative effective parameter count or show that this turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
